Hey guys, well I'm kinda new here and was requested to post some pics and a talk about my Earthbag house that I built. Some backstory... I was in a job I hated and had a lot of downtime. I watched a ton of videos on youtube to pass the time and ended up falling in love with earthbag construction. I liked the simplicity, the rock bottom price and the flexibility of the style so much that I had to try it. I own some Agricultural land in western oregon with no house or anything on it so it would be nice to not be in a tent every time I am out there anyway.
I bought about 1500 sandbags on Amazon. Some were a larger size (like a 35 lb dogfood bag) and others were the normal sandbag size that everyone has seen for flood control. I wanted the simplest strongest design so I just did a circle. I saw a long video from an outfit called Cal-earth on Youtube that was describing an ancient building method that used 2 ropes and 2 stakes to create a dome on top of a round building. I didn't really want this bee-hive looking building and sure as hell didn't want to lift bags 15 feet in the air to finish the roof so I used the method only part way to create a slightly inward sloping wall. This was a unique thing from what I have seen everyone else doing. I also use the largest bags for the first 4 vertical feet of wall (about 500 of them). Then switched to smaller bags. If you look closely at my building from the outside you can see this switch in a steeper angle of the outside wall but on the interior pics there is just a smooth sweeping curve. I aligned the smaller bags with the inside edge of the bags so the interior wall would be straight. There is 2 rows of barbwire between every set of bags which is traditional earthbag construction. I also made tampers with sticks/firewood and some nails. They worked really well and were free. I highly recommend.

The building was built on a rubble foundation where I scooped native soil out about 12" down the filled the entire hole with heavy crushed rock then finer rock/silt mix on the top. I did much of this work with a skidsteer... The center stake was pounded like 3 feet in and then cut off at about 2' high with a nail in the center. This was the dead-center point of the building. I started the rope off at exactly 10 feet so the inside edge of the wall at 2' would be 10' radius and 314 sq feet (pi for the win!) I wanted the first 2 feet of the wall to be vertical then start the curve inward so I hung a plumb from the 10' mark (knot) on the rope to lay the first of the bags. When I got to the 2' point I adjusted the knot for every row using another stake (same depth/top height) The placement of this stake was outside the wall at the door... The placement of this stake is important and described by the Cal-earth dome people. I am afraid to describe it more here and be wrong. PM me if you want details. The tie string of the bag was "flossed" through the crack between the placed bag and its neighbor. This was done so I would have 900 tie points inside and outside to hang chicken wire and stucco for an outer wall.

As the walls went up I integrated the 4x6 door frame into the main wall hardpoints (T's at door frame) by laying 2x4's with nails pounded in them after every 4 vertical bags. The bags were formed over the wood, nails and wire making a shockingly sturdy door frame. What you see in mine is insanely strong and far overbuilt. My windows were supposed to be arches but they ended up as triangles... Honestly they are shit and are a major problem. DO NOT MAKE WINDOWS WITHOUT A FORM. I was too exhausted/ out of time to unstack 20% of my building just to dick with a window so Im living with triangular windows. When I finally got to 6 feet I set up the laser level and was fucking amazed to see that I was within an inch of average level across the entire wall. I hadnâ€™t even been trying to do that it just happened. A testament to the simpler-is-better method of construction. A complete novice in awful conditions can build with these things perfectly the first time with minimal efforts almost by accident. Let that sink in a bit then think of other building methods.

At the top of the wall I carefully levelled everything wit the tamper then put on a 2x10 cap strip. I gave a lot of thought as to how I would do this part to increase structural integrity, provide anchors for the roof beams, etc. Remember, the top of the building at 7' high was tipping in almost a foot. What I mean is that a vertical string placed on the top edge of the wall would be about a foot in from the same place on the wall near the ground. This inward tipping wall was locking itself in place with tremendous force and was really strong. I laid my 2x10's all in place overlapping them so I could make perfectly matching cuts and cut the one farthest from the door first. I used its cut edges to scribe the next and so on. I always left about half an inch extra. I then drilled big holes in them and hammered 5/8" rebar down through them 4 feet into the wall. Essentially I pinned the upper wooden ring to the wall. Now remember when I said the wood ring was just a touch bigger than measured? Well when I pinned this in place this allowed me to make it all tight by pushing against the natural inward leaning nature of the bags. When I say its tight Im not kidding. I could not push a screwdriver between the wooden seams due to the pressure. Over all these seams I put nail plates adding strength and stability. On top of this I put a roof that looks like a traditional Chinese hat... Or maybe just a really wide cone. I ripped out the center stake dug a footing and filled with cement. Sunk a heavy j-bolt into the cement and let it dry. Next I put a big green ash pole that I I cut from a tree vertically on this bolt into a hole drilled on the butt and braced it with sticks. Chainsawed the top off to a final level and put 15' 2x6 rafters coming off of it over the wall with a hurricaine clip and down to a 4x4 post 5' from the outer wall. This gave me a fat overhang, double the roof space for rainwater collection and a porch all the way around the building. Sheathed this roof and the building was dried in. From there I had walls, a roof and gravel floor. I raked the floor into a slight dome and covered in plastic for a moisture barrier. covered that plastic in that pink 2" thick hard foam stuff from Home Depot. Over that I dry-laid paving bricks that I got at a used home store. It gave me a masonry floor that was fire proof damage proof nearly indestructible etc. In the places I walk I just put a few throw carpets.

I heat the place with a little wood stove and it only takes a little fire each day to stay warm in the winter. The 1-2 foot thick walls stay super cool in summer. I have some LED strip lights that I got on Amazon for like ten bucks that light the place and don't suck my solar system dry. The place is not a legal structure. I can't get home-owners insurance. or a mortgage. I can't even get an address which is interesting. I built it as a bit of a work camp as opposed to a permanent residence but it serves well enough for that as well. Below is the imgur links.
